CHAPTER I

QUINCY (1838-1848)

Under the shadow of Boston State House, turning its back on the house of John Hancock, the little passage called Hancock Avenue ran from Beacon Street, skirting the State House grounds, to Mount Vernon Street; and there, in the third house below Mount Vernon Place, February 16, 1838, a child was born, and christened later by his uncle, minister of the First Church after the tenets of Boston Unitarianism, as Henry Brooks Adams.

Had he been born in Jerusalem under the shadow of the Temple and circumcised in the Synagogue by his uncle the high priest, under the name of Israel Cohen, he would scarcely have been more distinctly branded; yet the ordinary traveller, who does not enter the field of racing, finds advantage in being ticketed through life, with the safeguards of an old, established traffic. Safeguards are often irksome, but sometimes convenient. A hundred years earlier, such safeguards as his would have secured any young man's success; although in 1838 their value was not what they had been in 1738, the mere accident of starting a twentieth-century career from a nest of associations so colonial—so troglodytic—as the First Church, the Boston State House, Beacon Hill, John Hancock and John Adams, Mount Vernon Street and Quincy, all crowding on ten pounds of unconscious babyhood, was so queer as to offer a subject of curious speculation to the baby long after.

He could not refuse to play his excellent hand. He accepted the situation as though he had been a party to it, and under the same circumstances would do it again, the more readily for knowing the exact values. To his life as a whole he was a consenting, contracting party and partner from the moment he was born to the moment he died. Only with that understanding—as a consciously assenting member in full partnership with the society of his age—had his education an interest.

As it happened, he never got to the point of playing the game at all; he lost himself in the study of it, watching the errors of the players; but this is the only interest in the story. A story of education—seventy years of it—the practical value remains to the end in doubt; but “although every one cannot be a Gargantua-Napoleon-Bismarck and walk off with the great bells of Notre Dame, every one must bear his own universe,” and most persons are moderately interested in learning how their neighbors have managed to carry theirs.

No such accident had ever happened before in human experience. For him, alone, the old universe was thrown into the ash-heap and a new one created. He and his eighteenth-century, troglodytic Boston were suddenly cut apart—separated forever—by the opening of the Boston and Albany Railroad; the appearance of the first Cunard steamers in the bay; and the telegraphic messages that carried from Baltimore to Washington the news that Clay and Polk were nominated for the Presidency. In May, 1844, when he was six years old, his new world was ready for use, and only fragments of the old met his eyes.

Of all this that was being done to complicate his education, he knew only the color of yellow. He first found himself sitting on a yellow kitchen floor in strong sunlight. The second lesson was taste. On December 3, 1841, scarlet fever all but carried him off; when he began to recover, he remembered clearly his aunt entering with a saucer and a baked apple. The third impression was discomfort: bundled in blankets and carried from Hancock Avenue to Mount Vernon Street, midwinter, January 10, 1842, stifling for want of air, while furniture groaned.

Scarlet fever, as a means of variation, counts for much. He fell behind his brothers in bone and height; his mind and character seemed to share in the fining-down of scale. He was not good in a fight; his nerves were more delicate than boys' nerves ought to be. He exaggerated these weaknesses as he grew older: the habit of doubt; of distrusting his own judgment and of rejecting the world's; the tendency to regard every question as open; the hesitation to act except as a choice of evils; the shirking of responsibility; the love of line, form, quality; the horror of ennui; the passion for companionship and the antipathy to society—qualities of New England character, stimulated by the fever. His brothers were the type; he was the variation.

Whatever was peculiar about him was education, not character, and came as the result of that eighteenth-century inheritance which he took with his name. The atmosphere was colonial, revolutionary, almost Cromwellian, steeped in the odor of political crime. Resistance to something was the law of New England nature; for numberless generations, his predecessors had viewed the world chiefly as a thing to be reformed, filled with evil forces to be abolished. Boys naturally look on all force as an enemy; the New Englander had learned also to love the pleasure of hating; his joys were few. “Politics, as a practice, whatever its professions, had always been the systematic organization of hatreds,” and Massachusetts politics had been as harsh as the climate.

The charm of New England was harshness of contrasts and extremes of sensibility—a cold that froze the blood, and a heat that boiled it—so that the pleasure of hating—one's self if no better victim offered—was not its rarest amusement. The double exterior nature gave life its relative values. Winter and summer, cold and heat, town and country, force and freedom, marked two modes of life and thought, balanced like lobes of the brain. Town was restraint, law, unity: winter confinement; school; rule; straight, gloomy streets piled with snow; thaws that made crossing perilous; uncles, aunts, and cousins who expected children to behave. Above all, winter represented the desire to escape and go free. Country, only seven miles away, was liberty, diversity, outlawry, the endless delight of sense impressions given by nature for nothing, and breathed by boys without knowing it.

Boys are wild animals, rich in the treasures of sense. To the boy Henry Adams, summer was drunken. Smell was the strongest—hot pine-woods and sweet-fern; new-mown hay; ploughed earth; box hedges; peaches, lilacs, syringas; stables and cow-yards; salt water and low tide on the marshes. Next came taste; they knew the taste of everything, from pennyroyal and flagroot to the shell of a pignut and the letters of a spelling-book—the taste of A-B, AB, suddenly revived on the boy's tongue sixty years afterwards. Light, line, and color were crude pleasures; New England light is glare, its atmosphere harshens color. His idea of pleasure in light was the blaze of sun; of color, a peony jewelled with morning dew; the intense blue of the sea from the Quincy hills; the cumuli of a June sky; the strong reds, greens, and purples of children's prints. The antipathies were the cold grays of November evenings and the thick, muddy thaws of a Boston winter. With such standards, the Bostonian could not but develop a double nature. Life was a double thing. After a January blizzard, the boy who stared with pleasure into the violent snow-glare, with its intense light and shade, scarcely knew what was meant by tone. He could reach it only by education.

Winter and summer bred two separate natures. Winter was always the effort to live; summer was tropical license. Whether rolling in grass, wading in brooks, swimming in the salt ocean, sailing in the bay, fishing for smelts, netting minnows, prowling pine-woods and quarries, chasing muskrats and turtles in swamps, or gathering mushrooms and nuts on autumn hills, summer and country were sensual living, while winter was compulsory learning. “Summer was the multiplicity of nature; winter was school.”

This division was the most decisive force he ever knew, running through life, marking its irreducible opposites, with growing emphasis to the last. Town and country, law and liberty, were hostile, and the man who pretended they were not, was in his eyes a schoolmaster—that is, a man employed to tell lies to little boys. Though Quincy was but two hours' walk from Beacon Hill, it belonged in a different world. For two hundred years, every Adams had lived within sight of State Street, yet none had taken kindly to the town, or been taken kindly by it. The boy inherited his double nature. Never for a moment did he connect the two ideas of Boston and John Adams; they were separate and antagonistic; the idea of John Adams went with Quincy.

Even a child felt Boston's social superiority and disliked it. Boston had bathrooms, a water-supply, a furnace, and gas; Quincy had none. The Brooks house in town was magnificent; the President's place at Quincy, larger and older and more interesting, smacked of colonial age but not of Boston plush. He never overcame the prejudice thus drawn with his breath; never could compel himself to care for nineteenth-century style, for he was born an eighteenth-century child. The old house at Quincy was eighteenth century; its Queen Anne panels and Louis Seize chairs were not comfortable for a boy, or for any one else. Nothing seemed to favor the older forms; most boys preferred the new, and the child felt himself at a disadvantage for the taste.

Attachment to Quincy was not altogether sentimental. Even there the curse of Cain set its mark. As though three or four energetic brothers and sisters were not enough to crush any child, every one else conspired towards an education he hated: order through chaos; discipline through freedom; unity through multiplicity. A boy's will is his life, and he dies when it is broken, as the colt dies in harness. Between him and his master has always been war.

All the more singular, then, that his first serious contact with the President—his grandfather—should have been a struggle of will that left no sting. He was six or seven; a passionate rebellion one summer morning against school reduced his mother to helplessness; at the bottom of the staircase to the President's library, the door opened; the old man, close on eighty, put on his hat, took the boy's hand, and walked with him, without a word, up the shadeless mile to town. The boy, paralyzed by awe, calculated dodges; the old man never stopped; the boy found himself seated in school, the centre of curious if not malevolent criticism; only then did the President release his hand and depart. The act ought to have earned hatred; it did not. The old man had shown no temper, made no display of force; above all, he had held his tongue. The boy gave him credit for intelligent silence, and admitted force as a form of right.

These summers the President admitted the child to a sort of intimacy that, when the child grew old, shocked him: haunting the library; deranging papers; ransacking drawers for foreign coins; drawing the sword-cane; snapping the travelling-pistols; upsetting corners; peering into the dressing-closet where inverted tumblers covered doomed caterpillars; provoking the Madam when cut-glass bowls were stolen to plant acorns and peachstones. Tree-culture was the President's hobby; he loved processes more than results; the boy's conscience brought him the finest peaches from the garden, eating only the less perfect by way of compensation. The role of schoolmaster perhaps pricked the old man's conscience; there exists a little volume of Nursery Rhymes with the boy's name in the President's trembling hand; there were the Bibles given at birth; their grandfather Brooks supplied the silver mugs.

A new cottage “on the hill,” five minutes' walk above “the old house,” with its far view over Quincy Bay and Boston, held these heirlooms and his childhood's pleasures. Before railways transformed the New England town, the parish church showed its bald-headed leading citizens on the main aisle. It was unusual for boys to sit behind a President grandfather and to read over his head the tablet to a President great-grandfather who had “pledged his life, his fortune, and his sacred honor.” Boys supposed that what had been would continue to be.

“You'll be thinkin' you'll be President too!”

The Irish gardener's remark struck him so strongly that he never forgot it. He had not thought on the subject; that there should be a doubt was the novelty.

The Madam was more remote, but more decorative; a delicate presence in her panelled room with Dutch tiles, her Queen Anne mahogany, her Sèvres, her little glass-doored case labelled with “Peregrine Pickle,” “Tom Jones,” “Hannah More.” She could never be Bostonian, which was her cross and her charm. She was born in London in 1775; driven by war to Nantes; brought back to London; her father Joshua Johnson, Consul of the United States; she married John Quincy in London, 1797; went to Berlin; to America; to St. Petersburg, leaving two boys behind and crossing Europe with a seven-year-old through the Cent Jours; to England again; to Washington as Secretary of State's wife; to the White House, four miserable years; to a long widowhood of public service as a Member's wife. By 1843–48, she was a vision of silver gray, presiding over her old President and her mahogany; hardly more Bostonian than on her wedding-day in the shadow of the Tower. The boy knew nothing of her interior stress; he might have felt a vague suspicion that from her he inherited the seeds of the primal sin, that he was half exotic: a quarter taint of Maryland blood. Charles Francis, half Marylander by birth, hardly saw Boston till school, and Boston took long to accept him.

A boy who began with inferior bone, a delicacy of mind and body, ought to have rebelled against the standards of the nineteenth century. The atmosphere of his first ten years was that of his grandfather's boyhood, barring Bunker Hill; the tone of Boston society was colonial; the true Bostonian knelt before English standards. The eighteenth century ruled society long after 1850, but the prehistoric stage ended abruptly with his tenth year. One winter morning, the word paralysis attached itself to the President seated in an invalid armchair by the spare bedroom fire. On February 21, 1848, the eighteenth century, as an actual companion, vanished. The scene on the floor of the House when the old man fell struck a boy whose boy-life faded with his grandfather's.

The funeral at Quincy, with its surroundings of national respect and family pride, might have ruined many a boy by much less. The clergyman's refined appearance, his dignity, cadence, English, and appreciation, gave to the service a character that left an overwhelming impression. Afterwards, the official ceremony in Faneuil Hall, where an oration, admirable as scholarship and eloquence, could not put the dead President in, deepened the lesson. The shadow of 1812 still hung over State Street; the shadow of Civil War already darkened Faneuil Hall. No rhetoric could reconcile Bostonians in the heart of mercantile Boston to the inherited quarrel of the Adamses with State Street, which had again and again broken into riot, bloodshed, foreign and civil war, banishment and confiscation, till Florence seemed hardly more turbulent than Boston. How whisper Hartford Convention there? What say of Secession?

Thus, at ten years old, the boy stood face to face with a dilemma. What was he?—where was he going? Something was wrong; it must be Boston. Quincy represented a moral principle—the principle of resistance to Boston. His Adams ancestors must have been right, since they were always hostile to State Street. If State Street was wrong, Quincy must be right! Turn as he pleased, he came back on the eighteenth century and the law of Resistance; of Truth; of Duty, and of Freedom. “He was a ten-year-old priest and politician.” He could not have guessed what the next fifty years had in store; sometimes, in old age, he wondered whether the clearest foreknowledge would have helped. Supposing he had seen a New York stock-list of 1900, and studied the statistics of railways, telegraphs, coal, and steel—would he have quitted his ancestral prejudices and abstract ideals, and asked for the fatted calf in State Street and a clerkship in the Suffolk Bank?

Sixty years afterwards he was still unable to make up his mind. Each course had its advantages; but the material advantages, looking back, seemed to lie wholly in State Street.
